chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from some of his companions, who said:

Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: It is permissible for a man to change his bequest — freeing the one whom he had ordered to be kept as a slave, and enslaving the one whom he had ordered to be freed, and giving to the one whom he had deprived, and depriving the one whom he had given to — for as long as he has not died.

key_terms.حَرَمَ: To deprive, to forbid, to exclude from a bequest
key_terms.عِتْق: Manumission, the freeing of an enslaved person — one of the most meritorious acts in Islamic law
key_terms.مِلْك: Ownership, possession, servitude — here referring to the enslaved status of the person
key_terms.وَصِيَّة: Bequest, will, testamentary disposition — a legally binding instruction that takes effect upon the testator's death

ai.seo_question: Can a person change or revoke their Islamic will (wasiyya) before death?
ai.summary: Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sajjad (AS), the fourth Imam, rules that a testator retains full discretion to revoke and reverse any or all provisions of his bequest at any point before death. This ruling establishes the fundamental principle that a will is ambulatory — it has no legal effect until death — so the testator may freely revoke manumissions, transfers of property, and bequests. In early Islamic jurisprudence, this was an important clarification distinguishing a bequest (wasiyya) from a completed gift (hiba), since a gift, once delivered, cannot be revoked.
word_analysis: to keep as a slave/to retain in ownership
